title: The Moral Certainty of Today’s Cruelty
author: Rory Bahadur
content:
One of the most dangerous falsities about American morality is that it exists
outside human interest, power and comfort. We like to believe morality is
stable, principled and universal. We imagine it as a bright line separating
right from wrong, justice from injustice, civilization from barbarism. [But
much of what we call morality is not moral
truth](https://www.amazon.com/Critical-Race-Approach-Systemic-
Inequity/dp/153103313X). It is moral convenience. It is the story power tells
after it wins.

That is why so much of today’s American politics feels morally upside down.
[Cruelty](https://www.amazon.com/Critical-Race-Approach-Systemic-
Inequity/dp/153103313X) toward immigrants can be described as restoring the
rule of law. Masked enforcement operations can be framed as public safety.
Detention without ordinary procedural protection can be defended as national
security. Protest can be called disorder when it challenges state power, but
patriotism when it serves the dominant political imagination. The conduct does
not speak for itself but rather power teaches us what to call it.

Americans understand this better than we admit. We [revere private
property](https://www.amazon.com/Critical-Race-Approach-Systemic-
Inequity/dp/153103313X) as almost sacred. We celebrate the landowner who says,
“Get off my property.” We build constitutional protection around the idea that
government may not take private land without compensation. In American
culture, property is identity, independence and moral entitlement. [But that
moral entitlement appeared only after the land was
taken](https://www.amazon.com/Critical-Race-Approach-Systemic-
Inequity/dp/153103313X). Before white ownership, Native possession was
dismissed as legally inferior, morally irrelevant or historically
inconvenient. After white ownership, the same land became sacred private
property. What had been conquest became title; violence became civilization
and theft became law.

The same pattern structures our present. [If Americans
imagined](https://www.amazon.com/Critical-Race-Approach-Systemic-
Inequity/dp/153103313X) foreign powers storming our neighborhoods, seizing our
neighbors, separating families and demanding submission in the name of order,
many would call resistance morally necessary. But when state power is directed
at people already coded as alien, threatening or disposable, [the moral
vocabulary changes](https://www.amazon.com/Critical-Race-Approach-Systemic-
Inequity/dp/153103313X). Fear becomes enforcement, humiliation becomes
deterrence and desperation becomes criminality. The suffering of the targeted
becomes the price of restoring order.

The point is not that law is meaningless or that violence should be excused.
The point is that our moral categories are far less consistent than we
pretend. We condemn in others what we sanctify in ourselves. We call our
violence tragic necessity and their violence proof of savagery. [We call our
domination law and their resistance terrorism, and the fraudulence of moral
absolutism allows us to avoid the agony of
comparison](https://www.amazon.com/Critical-Race-Approach-Systemic-
Inequity/dp/153103313X).

When we see suffering among people we have been taught to recognize, we feel
the full force of human grief. But when we witness suffering among people we
have been taught to distance, distrust or fear, it becomes abstraction.
Children coughing from tear gas, families afraid of masked agents, asylum
seekers trapped in detention, and communities living under threat of raids can
be made to disappear morally even when they are visible factually. [Our brains
sort humanity before morality](https://www.amazon.com/Critical-Race-Approach-
Systemic-Inequity/dp/153103313X) ever arrives such that some lives are vivid
and others become background.

This is [not hypocrisy](https://www.amazon.com/Critical-Race-Approach-
Systemic-Inequity/dp/153103313X) because hypocrisy implies we know what we are
doing. But our conclusions about morality appear obvious and forgone because
our moral instincts have already been organized by identity, familiarity and
power. That is why “terrorist,” “criminal,” “illegal,” “rioter,” “patriot,”
“freedom fighter” and “law-abiding citizen” are not merely descriptions.
Rather they are moral weapons telling us whose conduct must be understood and
whose conduct must be condemned before explanation begins.

The same moral fiction appeared during the [COVID
lockdowns](https://www.amazon.com/Critical-Race-Approach-Systemic-
Inequity/dp/153103313X). Many people treated shutting down large parts of
society as obviously moral and questioning that certainty was often cast as
indifference to human life. But the people most able to define that morality
were often the people least likely to bear its costs. For many professionals,
lockdown meant working from home, protecting themselves, and preserving their
income. For many lower-wage workers, it meant lost jobs, lost health
insurance, lost housing stability, and financial panic. That does not prove
the lockdowns were wholly wrong. It proves something more uncomfortable: moral
judgment is often shaped by power. Those with security can describe sacrifice
as civic duty when the sacrifice is imposed on those with less security. [When
the powerful announce morality and the vulnerable absorb the burden, moral
certainty becomes much easier](https://www.amazon.com/Critical-Race-Approach-
Systemic-Inequity/dp/153103313X).

That does not mean all moral claims are meaningless. But moral certainty is
dangerous because it lets ordinary people participate in cruelty without
feeling cruel. [It lets nations conquer while calling themselves
civilized](https://www.amazon.com/Critical-Race-Approach-Systemic-
Inequity/dp/153103313X), lets institutions exclude while calling themselves
fair and it lets societies rank human beings while calling the ranking
morality.

And it lets a political movement turn domination into virtue. That is why the
present moment is so revealing. The cruelty is not hidden. But morality makes
removal, punishment and exclusion feel righteous. Once immigrants become
invaders, protestors become mobs, racial justice becomes favoritism, women’s
autonomy becomes moral decay and inequality becomes deserved consequence, the
political work has already been done. [The public does not need to be
persuaded to tolerate cruelty because the reality of power dynamics teach us
to experience cruelty as order](https://www.amazon.com/Critical-Race-Approach-
Systemic-Inequity/dp/153103313X).

Ultimately morality is not the opposite of domination but is [one of
domination’s favorite disguises](https://www.amazon.com/Critical-Race-
Approach-Systemic-Inequity/dp/153103313X). For example, racial hierarchy has
rarely survived by saying, openly and honestly, “We wish to subordinate these
people.” [It survives by attaching moral meaning to the
hierarchy](https://www.amazon.com/Critical-Race-Approach-Systemic-
Inequity/dp/153103313X). The dominant group becomes civilized, responsible,
lawful, hardworking and deserving. The subordinated group becomes dangerous,
backward, dependent, immoral or ungrateful. Once that moral sorting occurs,
inequality no longer feels like oppression but feels like a natural result.

That is the mechanism we must confront. Not just bad laws, bad actors or open
prejudice. We must confront the [human
capacity](https://www.amazon.com/Critical-Race-Approach-Systemic-
Inequity/dp/153103313X) to convert self-interest into righteousness so quickly
that we never notice the conversion happened. The question is not whether we
have morals. Of course we do. The question is whether our morals are doing
what we think they are doing. Are they restraining cruelty, or licensing it?
Are they exposing power, or protecting it? Are they making us more humane, or
merely allowing us to feel humane while someone else pays the price?

Often, the most dangerous people are those most certain they are doing right.
Because once cruelty feels moral, there is almost no limit to what decent
people will justify.
